intro: Before you learn any state, you learn how we know. This module gives you the kinds of evidence, the tags, the rules for each source, the land the history happened on, and the first cases to practise on: early farming, Nok, early iron, the Bantu expansion and Jenne-jeno.
outcomes: Explain why European scholars denied Africa a history, and how the evidence answered them.
Name the kinds of evidence, one blind spot each, and apply the five tags to a claim.
Use the main rules for oral tradition, written sources, laboratory dates and language evidence.
Describe early farming, Nok, early iron and the Bantu expansion with the right caution.
Explain why Jenne-jeno matters, and rewrite a weak claim into a tagged one.

lessons.title: Why Africa's past was denied, and how historians answered

blocks.x: The denial that Africa had a history dates from the late eighteenth century. Hegel called Africa 'not a historical continent'. In 1923 A. P. Newton said history begins when people write, and in 1963 Hugh Trevor-Roper said there was only the history of Europeans in Africa. {{gha1-fage}} [FIRM]
Even colonial history was not African history: of the 68 chapters in the three general volumes of the Cambridge History of the British Empire, only four bear directly on Africa. {{gha1-fage}}
The belief that Africa had no history before Europeans is a claim about colonial-era sources, not about Africa. This course never treats a missing European record as a missing past.
The Hamitic myth

Seligman wrote in 1930 that 'the civilizations of Africa are the civilizations of the Hamites'. {{gha1-fage}} The idea came from an older German scheme of waves from Asia, each bringing a stage of civilisation, which Meinhof turned into a ranking of languages. {{gha1-olderogge}}

Greenberg showed that Hamitic can at most be a linguistic label, and that the languages once called Hamitic belong to a wider Afro-Asiatic family. His example is that Hausa, speaking an Afro-Asiatic language, were ruled by Fulani who speak a Niger-Congo one. So language does not map on to race, culture or rank. {{gha1-fage}} [FIRM]

The scheme collapsed between the wars, first with the 1924 discovery of Australopithecines in South Africa, then with East African finds that put the whole sequence of human evolution on the continent. {{gha1-olderogge}}
Two more myths: the unchanging village and the subsistence economy

Functionalist anthropology fixed each society on one plane before the conquest, by subtracting whatever looked like outside influence. It sought simple, isolated societies, took change to come only from outside, and stopped asking how a society had already changed. {{gha1-curtin}} [PROBABLE]
Historians' work showed that precolonial institutions, religions and economies changed as fast as other societies' did between the agricultural and industrial revolutions. {{gha1-curtin}}

No precolonial African community lacked trade. Many Saharan-fringe pastoralists earned half or more of their annual calories by exchanging animal products for cereals, and farmers sold surplus to pay for salt, cattle, shea butter, kola nuts or dates. {{gha1-curtin}} [PROBABLE]

Most of Africa was also literate in the sense that a class of scribes could read and write: Ge'ez in Ethiopia, Arabic across the north, the Sahara, the Sudanic belt and the east coast, and European languages of trade on the western coasts. Mass literacy was a post-industrial development everywhere. {{gha1-curtin}} [FIRM]
The answer: African historians and a new method

African authors wrote their own histories long before the universities: Reindorf on the Gold Coast and Asante (1895), Samuel Johnson on the Yoruba (completed 1897, published 1921), Kagwa in Uganda from 1906, and Egharevba's Short History of Benin (1934). {{gha1-fage}}

blocks.title: How the method changed
head: Date
Event
Why it matters
rows: Murdock calls indigenous oral traditions 'completely undependable'
The position the next step answered. {{gha1-curtin}}
Vansina's Oral Tradition sets critical controls; a Dakar seminar stresses oral tradition, linguistics and archaeology together
Dike holds a history chair at Ibadan
The Unesco General History project begins
A continent-wide synthesis written largely by Africans. {{gha1-fage}}

blocks.x: The Unesco General History was planned by an International Scientific Committee of 39 members, two-thirds African. Every chapter went to the whole committee, and the History aims to show divergent views rather than hide them; each chapter's views are its author's. {{gha5-front}} [PROBABLE] So when its chapters disagree, this course sets them side by side.

The answer to the denial can overshoot. Later writers, African and European alike, sometimes built a glorious past to answer European superiority. {{gha1-fage}} And pointing only to kingdoms argues on the opponents' terms: the stateless society, based on co-operation more than coercion, was probably one of Africa's great achievements in law and politics. {{gha1-curtin}} [CONTESTED]

blocks.q: A 1960s lecture says Africa has no history because Africans did not write. Which reply uses the evidence best?
o: Agree, then study Europeans in Africa
Scribal literacy existed across much of Africa, and oral tradition, archaeology and linguistics recover the past where writing is absent
Change the subject to Egypt only
blocks.w: The premise is wrong on literacy, and the method answers the rest. {{gha1-curtin}}

blocks.q: A source claims a West African city was founded by 'Hamites' because its rulers spoke an Afro-Asiatic language. What is the flaw?
o: Hamitic is at most a language label; language does not map on to race or origin, as Hausa speakers ruled by Fulani show
blocks.w: Greenberg's Hausa-Fulani case breaks the equation. {{gha1-fage}}

i: The 'no history' claim was a claim about European sources. {{gha1-fage}}
The Hamitic myth fails on Greenberg's evidence: language is not race.
Precolonial societies traded and changed; 'static' and 'subsistence only' are myths. {{gha1-curtin}}

lessons.title: Kinds of evidence, the tags, and why strong claims need two

blocks.x: African history before 1880 is rebuilt from five kinds of evidence: archaeology, historical linguistics, oral tradition, written sources and material heritage. Genetics is a sixth and newer line. {{lib}} {{nature-bantu}}
No source is ranked in advance. Each is a message from the past with its own intentions, so each needs criticism, and each can lead to the others. {{gha1-intro}} [FIRM]

blocks.title: Evidence kinds and their blind spots
head: Kind
Good for
Blind spot
rows: Rarely says what people called themselves or how they were governed
Showing how related languages split and spread
Shows that a vocabulary was shared, not when or how many people moved
Compressed genealogies, a floating gap, and tellers who shape the past for present politics
Outsiders relied on informants and had their own aims
Must be read with archaeology, not instead of it

blocks.x: Looting makes the archaeological blind spot worse, because an object without a find-spot has lost most of its meaning. {{icom-redlist}} {{nok-franke}}
The tag system

blocks.title: The evidence tags used throughout this course
head: Tag
Meaning
rows: Well attested in several independent kinds of evidence
Most specialists accept it, with some uncertainty
Historians disagree, so both sides are given
From oral or chronicle tradition, so approximate
Few sources survive, or they are late or one-sided

blocks.x: A claim with no tag is background that is not in dispute. When you meet a number, ask who counted it and how. {{lib}}
Combining sources

The 'master source' differs by topic and may be known only after the work is done; for prehistory there is no written record at all. Al-Bakri's account of Koumbi Saleh is incomplete without excavation, and oral tradition led archaeologists to the site. {{gha1-kizerbo15}} [FIRM]

The Sao of Lake Chad show what combining achieves. Oral tradition, a few Arabic manuscripts, excavation and carbon-14 dating together turned a legendary people into an authenticated one: the Mdaga mound in Chad was occupied for nearly 2,500 years, a result no single source could have produced. {{gha1-obenga}} [PROBABLE]

blocks.title: Worked example: dating the circular ruins of the Lobi country
steps: A text by de Barros suggested a Portuguese origin, but the line of the supposed road and a plaster coating that was too fresh ruled that out.
The Wiili and Birifor name for the ruins, kol na wo, means 'stables for foreigners' cows', which points to a stock-keeping outsider.
The pottery style identified the outsiders as the Koulango, and the migration traditions of the neighbouring peoples then gave an estimated date.
No single source settled it; four conflicting or supporting clues did. {{gha1-kizerbo15}}

blocks.x: Beware the 'psychosis of precision'. Why say Koumbi Saleh fell in 1086 rather than at the end of the eleventh century? Eclipses and external events give fixed points; a bare year from a reign count does not. {{gha1-intro}} [TRADITIONAL DATE]

blocks.q: Which pairing of evidence would make the strongest claim?
o: Two archaeological digs by the same team
Archaeology plus an independent line such as linguistics or a written source
blocks.w: Strong claims need more than one kind of evidence, gathered independently. {{lib}}

blocks.q: A timeline states 'Koumbi Saleh fell in 1086'. Which wording should replace it?
o: Koumbi Saleh fell on a date that is unknowable
Koumbi Saleh declined towards the end of the eleventh century
blocks.w: Reign counts and oral dates cannot support a single year. {{gha1-intro}}

i: Five main kinds of evidence, plus genetics; each has a blind spot another can cover. {{lib}}
Every claim carries a tag that tells you how strong it is.
Combining independent sources turns legend into history, as at Mdaga. {{gha1-obenga}}

lessons.title: Oral tradition: rules for a spoken source

blocks.x: Oral tradition is not rumour. In the Mande world, specialist remembrancers called jeli, or griots, keep structured accounts, and griots form a hereditary group that has acted as historian, musician, mediator and court spokesperson. {{griot-brit}} {{hale-griot}} {{wiki-oral}}

A tradition is a testimony passed by word of mouth from one generation to the next, and a valid one should rest on an eyewitness account. Rumour is excluded, because it depends on hearsay. {{gha1-vansina}} [FIRM]

The test resembles Islamic hadith criticism, which asked of each link in a chain of informants whether the person could have known, understood and passed on the report, and whether they had a reason to distort it. {{gha1-vansina}}

blocks.title: Four forms of oral tradition and what each lets you do
head: Form
How it is made
Historian's use and limit
rows: Learned by heart, no special rules: names, titles, proverbs, genealogies, prayers
Can be built on word for word, but interpolation is easy. {{gha1-vansina}}
Learned by heart with formal rules, including songs
Most precisely transmitted, but allusive; needs a commentary. {{gha1-vansina}}
Variants probably descend from one original, but no archetype can be rebuilt. {{gha1-vansina}}
Freely recast, so collect every variant, including neighbours' versions. {{gha1-vansina}}

blocks.x: Three rules from the social side

i: Every tradition has a 'social surface', an institution that needs it; a tradition no one needs is dropped. {{gha1-vansina}}
A tradition that goes against its own interest is more likely true: a people saying it is younger than another, or a royal chronicle admitting defeat. {{gha1-vansina}}
Know the audience. Among the Gouro an open lineage version coexists with a closed secret-society version. {{gha1-intro}}

blocks.x: Rival versions are a safeguard: when Bambara and Fula griots from opposing camps agree, the point is strengthened. {{gha1-intro}} [PROBABLE]
Who is telling? Griot and knower

In the savanna of former French West Africa, a dieli (griot) is a musician, genealogist and praise-singer with licence to embellish, while a doma is an initiated master of knowledge, bound not to lie, who names his teachers back through a chain. People ask, 'is it a dieli story or a doma story?' {{gha1-bah}} [PROBABLE]

That picture of the truthful doma is a member's statement of the tradition's ideal, and even careful traditions are tidied by social pressure. Use it to explain why informants cite a chain, not to claim that an initiated informant cannot err. {{gha1-bah}} {{gha1-vansina}} [CONTESTED]
Dates from genealogies, and how lists get tidied

An average dynastic generation runs 26 to 32 years, but average reign length varies too much to use. A date projected back from a first written date should carry a mark, for example 'c. 1635' for the founding of the Kuba kingdom. {{gha1-vansina}} [FIRM]
Succession rules change the average: Yatenga's brother-to-brother succession yields a different reign length from Ouagadougou's father-to-son succession. {{gha1-kizerbo15}}

King lists are shortened or stretched. Segmentary societies drop 'useless' ancestors; usurpers are left out; in the Great Lakes region father-to-son successions appear far more often than anywhere else in the world, a sign of tidying; and colonial indirect rule rewarded longer dynasties. Irregularities are therefore often the best guarantee of authenticity. {{gha1-vansina}} [PROBABLE]
Checking a tradition against other evidence

Independence must be proved. Merchant caravans carried stories between peoples, and the first African-written histories, such as Johnson's on Oyo and Kagwa's on Buganda, shaped later dynastic lists. {{gha1-vansina}}
If an oral claim conflicts with an archaeological object, the object wins. Written texts are usually better on quantities, oral accounts on motives. {{gha1-vansina}} [PROBABLE]

Collected traditions mostly concern the nineteenth century and rarely reach back before 1700. Oral tradition is a first-class source for the last few centuries, poor for dates and numbers, and before that a helper to archaeology. Cite each oral source separately; 'tradition has it that' is a dangerous generalisation. {{gha1-vansina}} [FIRM]
Counting time without a calendar

blocks.title: Ways the past was counted without a written calendar
head: Device
Example
What it gives the historian
rows: Alladians of Moosou keep five generations, each ruling nine years. {{gha1-hama}}
History traced back to about the eighteenth century in societies without kings.
In the Sudanese savanna age is given in rainy seasons. {{gha1-hama}}
Seven-day week, six-week month, nine-month year, realigned on the sun. {{gha1-hama}}
An event can be placed in a month of a named ruler's reign [CONTESTED].

blocks.x: How a society counts time reflects its economy and way of life, not an essential 'African nature': clock-and-money time in towns differs from time in the countryside. Avoid any sentence that says Africans 'think of time as' one thing. {{gha1-hama}} [FIRM]

A folk tale is not oral tradition in this sense. Woodson's 1928 school reader names no teller, date or collector, so a king named inside one of its tales is not evidence that the king existed. {{wood-tales}}

blocks.q: Two clans tell their origins. Clan A says it arrived first and founded the town; clan B admits it arrived later as clients of A. Which claim deserves more weight?
o: Clan A's, because founders remember best
Clan B's, because it goes against the teller's own interest
blocks.w: A tradition that runs against its teller's interest has resisted the pull of flattery. {{gha1-vansina}}

blocks.q: A king list has 20 rulers and the average reign in the twentieth century was 20 years. Should you date the founding to 400 years ago?
o: Yes, that is the standard method
No: succession rules change the average, so mark any such date as calculated and approximate
Yes, if you add ten per cent
No: king lists are always invented
blocks.w: Yatenga's and Ouagadougou's successions give different averages. {{gha1-kizerbo15}} {{gha1-vansina}}

i: Treat oral tradition as a structured source with a point of view. {{gha1-vansina}}
Weigh rival versions, admissions against interest, and who is telling.
Mark calculated dates; when an object and a tradition clash, the object wins.

lessons.title: Written sources: who wrote, from where, and why

blocks.x: Three families of written source

i: Internal sources written in Africa: Ge'ez inscriptions and manuscripts, the Arabic chronicles written in Timbuktu, and ajami, which means African languages written in Arabic script. {{ajami-souag}} {{timbuktu-chron}}
External Arabic sources: al-Bakri, al-Umari and Ibn Battuta. {{arabic-geog}} {{fordham-ibnb}}
European sources: Portuguese, Dutch and British. Outside authors often relied on informants and had their own aims. {{lib}}

blocks.x: Early outside authors from Herodotus to Leo Africanus describe the Africa they could learn about, but do not study change over time, and it is often unclear whether a statement was seen, heard from a witness, or copied. {{gha1-fage}} [FIRM]
Reading an Arabic geographer

blocks.title: Questions to ask of an Arabic geographer
head: Question
Why it matters
rows: How much is reality, and how much a stock literary theme?
Fixed stories about the black world travel from book to book. {{gha1-djait}}
Few original reports exist: Ya'qubi (d. 897), Mas'udi, Ibn Hawqal (fl. 977) and a handful more. {{gha1-djait}}
Read the text from inside as well as outside, rejecting both blanket distrust and blanket trust. {{gha1-djait}}

blocks.x: A list that stops at the twelfth century counts 40 authors who speak of black Africa, 21 of them geographers. {{gha1-djait}}

Central and southern Africa have a void in written sources before the fifteenth century, and Arabic sources, which stress the Sudanic belt, can make it look like the only centre of organised states. Do not judge a region by its documents, and do not ignore the documents there are. {{gha1-djait}} [FIRM]
Histories written in Africa

blocks.title: Early written histories from Africa, and what each is
head: Work
What it is
How to use it
rows: Tarikh al-Sudan and Tarikh al-Fattash (Timbuktu, essentially 17th century)
Detailed on recent events, with critical comment on oral traditions of Ghana and Mali. {{gha1-fage}}
Strongest African-written sources for the Songhai period.
Little more than written-down tradition; the Kano text is not known in written form before about the 19th century. {{gha1-fage}}
Arabic literacy beyond the Islamised heartlands; Wilks found hundreds of Arabic texts in Ghana. {{gha1-fage}}
Evidence that writing was local, not only Saharan.
A continuous Ge'ez and then Amharic tradition of about two thousand years. {{gha1-fage}}
The one long written historical tradition south of the Sahara before 1500.

blocks.x: Ibn Khaldun (1332 to 1406) is the first real historian of the region. He sets out a cycle in which desert nomads conquer settled lands and their dynasty weakens after about three generations, and insists that scraps of information do not carry equal weight. His chapter on Mali rests partly on oral tradition of his day. {{gha1-fage}} [PROBABLE]
After 1500: new kinds of writing

From the early sixteenth century letters, reports and deeds appear alongside travellers' accounts, and Africans south of the Sahara begin to write their own history, first in Arabic, then in their own languages in Arabic script (Kiswahili, Hausa, Fulfulde, Malagasy and others), then in Latin script. {{gha1-hrbek}} [FIRM]

The Vai script was invented about 1833 by Momolu Duwalu Bukele, and nearly all Vai used it by 1900 for letters, accounts and customary law. {{gha1-hrbek}} The Asantehenes' Muslim scribes wrote letters in Arabic at a non-Muslim court. {{gha1-hrbek}}

Later is not more objective. Burton and Stanley were prisoners of the idea of white superiority, as Portuguese writers were of the superiority of their faith, so a nineteenth-century traveller is not automatically more credible than one from three centuries earlier. Yet a traveller's dated meeting can anchor a whole oral chronology. {{gha1-hrbek}} [PROBABLE]

Colonial records were made by foreigners and carry their view of themselves and of those they ruled, so even colonial history needs oral interviews. {{gha1-curtin}} [FIRM] The rule for every archive is the same: ask who made the record and for whom.

blocks.q: An essay quotes the Kano Chronicle as an eyewitness record of eleventh-century Kano. What is wrong?
o: It is little more than written-down tradition, not known in written form before about the nineteenth century
It is a Songhai tarikh about Gao
blocks.w: Unlike the Timbuktu tarikhs it does not criticise its traditions. {{gha1-fage}}

blocks.q: A student says the Sudanic belt was the only part of Africa with organised states before 1450, because that is where the Arabic sources describe states. What is the flaw?
o: Documents show where writers looked, not where states existed; central and southern Africa lack such texts
blocks.w: Absence of writing is not absence of states. {{gha1-djait}}

i: Sort a written source: internal, external Arabic or European. {{lib}}
Ask whether it was seen, heard or copied, and for whom it was written. {{gha1-fage}}
Missing documents are a gap in the record, not in the past. {{gha1-djait}}

lessons.title: Dates, words and genes: what the laboratory and linguists can prove

blocks.x: Laboratory dates
Materials must be identified by chemistry or X-ray, not by eye: copper is often mistaken for bronze and bronze for brass, and the difference matters for dating. {{gha1-iskander}} [FIRM]

blocks.title: Dating methods and their limits
head: Method
What it dates
Limit
rows: Organic remains up to about 70 000 years
Older samples need correction; dates on charcoal or wood date when the tree was cut, not when people used it. {{gha1-iskander}}
About plus or minus 10 per cent; but pottery is common, and the event dated is the firing. {{gha1-iskander}}

blocks.x: A flat stretch in the radiocarbon calibration curve, the so-called Hallstatt plateau of roughly 800 to 400 BCE, makes dates in that window imprecise. {{intcal20}} That matters for early iron in this module.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a corrected radiocarbon date
steps: Reeds from the First Dynasty mastaba of Qaa' at Saqqara gave an uncorrected radiocarbon date of 2450 plus or minus 65 before our era.
With the Stuiver-Suess correction the date became 2928 plus or minus 65 before our era, against a historical date of about 2900 before our era.
So the uncorrected date was about 480 years too young (our arithmetic: 2928 minus 2450), and a raw date for an old sample should be corrected before use. {{gha1-iskander}}

blocks.x: Chemistry also traces trade: obsidian found in Predynastic Egypt matches Ethiopian obsidian, which implies early contact. {{gha1-iskander}} [PROBABLE]

Where there is no stratigraphy, archaeologists have tended to coin new culture names from thin statistics, so lists of 'cultures' a few kilometres apart may later prove artificial. Use such names as labels for tool-kits, not as peoples. {{gha1-debono}} [PROBABLE]
What words can and cannot prove

Languages can be grouped by descent from a common stock (genetic), by shared structure (typological) or by present location (geographical). Only the first shows history, and a valid comparison must use a language's own words, not borrowings. {{gha1-diagne}} [FIRM]
Swahili is the classic trap: some varieties have over 60 per cent of their vocabulary borrowed from Arabic, which would wrongly make it Semitic. {{gha1-diagne}}

Only resemblances in both sound and meaning, in roots and grammatical markers, count as evidence of descent; shared tone or shared gender does not, because those features arise independently. {{gha1-greenberg}} [FIRM] Short look-alike words are common by chance, so a single resemblance proves nothing without regular sound correspondences across many words. {{dio-method-006}}

Greenberg's classification of 1949 to 1963 ended with four families: Niger-Kordofanian, Afro-Asiatic, Nilo-Saharan and Khoisan. {{gha1-greenberg}} His intermediate groups, such as Benue-Congo, Kwa and Gur, have never been adequately demonstrated, so treat them with reservation. {{gha1-greenberg}} [CONTESTED]

Glottochronology assumes basic vocabulary changes at a fixed rate, with Swadesh's retention rate put at 81 to 85 per cent for each thousand years, but borrowing makes the results fall short. Mark any number of years derived from vocabulary percentages as an estimate. {{gha1-diagne}} [CONTESTED]
Place names are a safer tool: villages ending in dugu mark Mande movement, saare Fulani settlement, ker Wolof and daaru Arabo-Berber. {{gha1-diagne}} [PROBABLE]

Language can follow marriage. The Dagomba horsemen who came to the Volta basin in the fourteenth century probably lost their own language to that of the Kusase women they married. {{gha1-kizerbo15}} Language, physical type and way of life must not be confused: African Americans kept their physical type but lost their languages within a generation or two. {{gha1-olderogge}} [PROBABLE]
What genes can and cannot prove

Y-chromosome haplogroup E, perhaps 50,000 years old and probably of eastern tropical African origin, is the commonest in all four quadrants of Africa, so the continent's regions are connected through male descent and the Sahara was never a biological boundary. {{gha9-keita}}
A male-line marker is one slice of ancestry and does not show skin colour or the whole population. The word race should be rejected on scientific and ethical grounds. {{gha9-keita}} [PROBABLE]

Blood-group studies show more variation within so-called races than between them: over 85 per cent of variation lies within nations and about 7 per cent between traditional races. {{gha1-diagne}} [PROBABLE]

blocks.q: A blog argues that Swahili is a Semitic language because so many of its words come from Arabic. What is the best reply?
o: Borrowed words do not show descent; Swahili's structure and core vocabulary are Bantu
blocks.w: Valid comparison uses a language's own heritage, not its borrowings. {{gha1-diagne}}

blocks.q: A charcoal sample from a furnace gives a radiocarbon date of 650 BCE. What two cautions apply?
o: It dates the tree, not the smelt, and it falls on the 800 to 400 BCE plateau, so the calendar date is imprecise
It is too young to date
blocks.w: Old wood and the Hallstatt plateau both blur early iron dates. {{gha1-iskander}} {{intcal20}}

i: Identify materials by analysis; correct old radiocarbon dates; watch the 800 to 400 BCE plateau. {{gha1-iskander}}
Only sound-and-meaning matches in core words show descent. {{gha1-greenberg}}
One genetic marker is one slice of ancestry, not a race. {{gha9-keita}}

lessons.title: The land, the Sahara and the first farmers

blocks.x: Geography impeded or promoted human activity but did not determine it; each community answered its surroundings in its own way. {{gha1-diarra}} [FIRM]

Africa covers about 30 million square kilometres, stretches about 8,000 kilometres from north to south, and has a smooth coast with few harbours. The East African Rift runs about 4,000 kilometres from the Red Sea to Mozambique, and its valleys played a remarkable role in the movement of peoples. {{gha1-diarra}} [FIRM]

blocks.title: Climate bands that explain where people farmed, herded and traded
head: Zone
Rainfall
What it means for history
rows: Dense forest, hard to farm and travel. {{gha1-diarra}}
Open woodland suited to farming and herding. {{gha1-diarra}}

blocks.x: The tsetse belt kept large livestock out of many farming areas, so there were few draught animals and little use of the wheel. {{gha1-mabogunje}} [PROBABLE]

Africa's isolation by an 'inhospitable coast' is exaggerated. The Mediterranean coast served centuries of exchange, the Indian Ocean monsoons carried ships to and from East Africa every year, and the Atlantic was little used before the fifteenth century because sailing ships could not beat the southward trade winds. {{gha1-diarra}} [CONTESTED]
The Sahara before the desert

No part of the Sahara has a stratigraphy good enough for a precise sequence, and apart from the Neolithic there are no absolute dates. By about 1000 before our era it was already desert. {{gha1-hugot}} [FIRM]

Domesticated shorthorn cattle appear at Uan Muhuggiag in Libya from about 5590 BCE and at Adrar Bous in Aïr about 3830 to 3790 BCE, which Andah argues is earlier than in the Nile Valley, so the cattle did not come from Egypt. The chapter does not say whether these dates are calibrated, so treat them as approximate. {{gha2-westafr}} [PROBABLE]

Tools do not prove farming. Agriculture needs pollen, traces of cultivated land or identifiable plant remains, because hoes and grinders may have dug clay or ground pigment. On most Saharan Neolithic sites the only plants found are wild, so stock-raisers, not farmers, followed the hunter-gatherers almost everywhere. {{gha1-hugot}} [FIRM]

Dhar Tichitt in south-east Mauritania is the clear exception: dry-stone villages with fortifications from about 2000 before our era, with millet grains showing that people ate millet from 1500 before our era. {{gha1-hugot}} [PROBABLE]
At Tichitt the share of pearl millet in the grain jumped from 3 to 60 per cent about 1000 before our era. {{gha1-shaw}}
African crops

Wheat and barley are winter-rain crops that cannot easily be grown south of the intertropical front, so West African cereals came from local grasses. Sorghum was domesticated by the first half of the second millennium before our era between the Sahara and the savanna from the Nile to Lake Chad, with pearl millet, finger millet and African rice following. {{gha1-shaw}} [PROBABLE]

blocks.title: What was domesticated where
head: Centre
Crops
Note
rows: Sorghum, pearl millet, fonio, African rice, Bambara groundnut, shea
The central Niger delta is the primary centre for African rice. {{gha1-porteres}}
Forest horticulture of tubers and tree crops. {{gha1-porteres}}
Teff, ensete, Arabian coffee, niger seed
Shares wheats and barleys with the Near East. {{gha1-porteres}}
Wheat and barley via Egypt; banana, taro and greater yam via East Africa
Bananas helped farming gain a foothold in the forest. {{gha1-porteres}}

blocks.x: Crops also travelled out of Africa: millet and finger millet are attested archaeologically in India about 1000 years before our era. {{gha1-obenga}} [PROBABLE]

blocks.title: When did African farming begin? Three readings
head: Reading
Date offered
How to treat it
rows: The end of the Pleistocene, between 9000 and 5000 before our era, offered as an opinion awaiting archaeology {{gha1-porteres}}
Sorghum by the first half of the second millennium before our era {{gha1-shaw}}
The only clear Saharan farming is millet at Tichitt from about 1500 before our era {{gha1-hugot}}

blocks.q: A Saharan site has grindstones and hoe-like tools but no plant remains. How should you describe it?
o: Not yet shown to be farming: only plant remains, pollen or fields prove cultivation
A nomad camp with no tools
blocks.w: Tools can serve other uses; millet at Tichitt is the clear exception. {{gha1-hugot}}

blocks.q: A textbook says 'Africa's geography cut it off from the world'. Which correction is best supported?
o: Relative, not absolute: Mediterranean and Indian Ocean trade ran for centuries, and the Atlantic was unused mainly because of the winds
Africa was never isolated in any way
blocks.w: Geography limited contact but did not prevent it. {{gha1-diarra}}

i: Geography set limits but did not decide outcomes. {{gha1-diarra}}
Farming needs plant evidence, not tools; Tichitt millet is the clear Saharan case. {{gha1-hugot}}
Sorghum, millets, African rice, yams and teff are African domesticates. {{gha1-porteres}}

lessons.title: Nok, early iron and the Bantu expansion

blocks.x: Nok

Nok culture is known from terracotta figures, often with elaborate heads, found around the Jos Plateau in central Nigeria. They date mainly to the first millennium BCE and the early centuries CE [PROBABLE]. {{nok-franke}} The culture is named after the village of Nok, where a tin miner found the first head in 1928, and Bernard Fagg identified the culture in the 1940s. {{nok-britannica}} {{nok-oro}}

The figurines come mostly from tin-mining gravels, which bracket them between 500 before our era and 200 of our era; a thermoluminescence date gives 620 plus or minus 230 before our era. The finds extend about 480 kilometres. {{gha1-shaw}} [PROBABLE]

Almost nothing is known of Nok politics, language or religion [THIN EVIDENCE]. Most figures were looted, so many lack context. {{gha2-westafr}} Excavations led by Goethe University Frankfurt have since recovered securely dated settlement and iron-working evidence. {{nok-franke}}

Some art historians see in the figurines the ancestry of Yoruba art 1,000 years later and 640 kilometres away. {{gha1-shaw}} Claims that the Nok were the ancestors of a named modern people, such as the Yoruba, are unproven. {{nok-breunig-2026}} [CONTESTED]
Early iron: where did it come from?
Iron smelting appears in West and Central Africa in the first millennium BCE. Whether it was invented independently or came across the Sahara is [CONTESTED]. {{gha2-westafr}} {{gha9-bocoum}}

West Africa was hardly touched by a Bronze Age: nearly 130 copper objects come from Mauritania, and Akjoujt copper dates to the fifth century before our era. {{gha1-shaw}} Iron ore, by contrast, is widespread: ferruginous laterite covers large areas of the savanna, while copper and tin were localised. {{gha1-mabogunje}} [PROBABLE]

blocks.title: Positions on the origin of West African iron
head: Position
Claim and evidence
Status
rows: With no earlier metallurgy, independent invention is unlikely; Taruga's smelting sites date from the fifth to the third century before our era, and the knowledge came from the Carthaginian sphere, perhaps via the Garamantes, not from Meroë. {{gha1-shaw}}
Nok people were working iron by 500 BCE and probably before; the beginning was largely indigenous. {{gha2-westafr}}

Claimed second-millennium dates, including Oboui in the Central African Republic at about 2343 to 1900 BCE; he concedes the Afunfun furnace in Niger rested on burned tree stumps mistaken for furnaces. {{gha9-bocoum}}
Meroë's role in spreading iron is not as obvious as used to be thought; iron may have spread along Saharan routes instead. {{gha1-vercoutter}}

blocks.x: How to choose: prefer the claim that rests on dated furnaces and calibrated radiocarbon, remember that charcoal dates the tree, and expect the 800 to 400 BCE plateau to blur the order of the earliest sites. {{intcal20}} {{gha1-iskander}}
The Bantu expansion

About 500 Bantu languages share a common ancestor that linguists place in the Cameroon and Nigeria borderland. Counts range from about 440 to 680 depending on how dialects are distinguished. {{oxbib-bantu}}

A dated language tree of 424 Bantu languages tied to three archaeological anchors puts the Bantu branch at about 4,800 years ago, the homeland in the savannah of north-western Cameroon, and the main line south-east along the edge of the rainforest, following savannah corridors. {{grollemund-001}} [PROBABLE]

An older estimate places proto-Bantu between about 1000 BCE or earlier and 400 BCE, a farming community with yams and cereals and only the goat, without metal. {{gha3-bantu}} So the date of the first split is [CONTESTED].

The older story of one great migration of conquering iron-users is largely abandoned. Language spread need not mean mass migration: at low population densities the expansion was small numbers moving from village to village, and agriculture and iron spread gradually. {{gha3-bantu}} [PROBABLE]
Bantu speech does not by itself mean ironworking: the Portuguese found Bubi speakers on Fernando Po who spoke a Bantu language yet did not know iron. {{gha1-olderogge}}

blocks.title: Old and current pictures of the Bantu expansion
head: Question
Older account
Current picture
rows: Small groups, mixing with existing populations {{gha3-bantu}}
Along the rainforest edge and savannah corridors, with an early split through the forest disputed {{grollemund-001}}
Spread at different times; Bantu speakers without iron existed {{gha1-olderogge}}

blocks.x: What counts as a migration?

Farmers moved fields and villages often, about every ten years on average, and herders moved with the seasons, so ordinary mobility is not 'migration'. A migration is the movement of whole communities at least the size of a village. {{gha5-vansina}} [PROBABLE]

The old picture of peoples pushing each other like billiard balls almost never happened. Most movements were slow expansion, trade diasporas, small warrior bands or a single founding elite; true mass migration is rare. {{gha5-vansina}} [CONTESTED]
Bantu is a language family, not a race or a tribe. Never write 'the Bantu tribe'. A 'Bantu myth' could grow as the Hamitic myth did. {{gha3-bantu}}

blocks.q: A documentary says: 'The Nok were the first people in sub-Saharan Africa to smelt iron.' Which correction is best supported?
o: None is needed: Nok has the oldest dates
Say Nok is among the early iron-using cultures; other sites have early claims and the radiocarbon plateau blurs 800 to 400 BCE
Say iron came only from Carthage
Say Nok had no iron at all
blocks.w: Nok is among the early iron-using cultures [PROBABLE], but 'first' cannot be supported [CONTESTED]. {{gha2-westafr}} {{gha9-bocoum}}

blocks.q: A textbook says 'wherever Bantu languages spread, ironworking went with them'. Which case tests that claim best?
o: The Bubi of Fernando Po, who spoke a Bantu language but had no iron
blocks.w: Language and technology must not be confused. {{gha1-olderogge}}

blocks.q: A website says the Yoruba descend directly from the Nok because both made fine terracotta heads. What is the main flaw?
o: Style alone cannot show descent, and Nok language and identity are unknown
blocks.w: A likeness of style across 1,000 years is not a family tree. {{gha1-shaw}}

i: Nok is famous for terracotta, but its society is mostly unknown [THIN EVIDENCE]. {{gha2-westafr}}
Early iron is real; whether it was invented locally or came from the north is [CONTESTED].
Bantu names a language family spread by small groups over centuries, not one conquest. {{gha3-bantu}}

lessons.title: Jenne-jeno: a city without a king

blocks.x: Jenne-jeno lies in the inland Niger delta in Mali. Excavations by Susan and Roderick McIntosh show a town occupied from about 250 BCE, growing into a dense urban cluster with a town wall in the first millennium CE. It grew without an obvious king or palace, and before regular trans-Saharan trade [PROBABLE]. {{penn-jj}} {{ehraf-jj}} {{mcintosh-memoir}} {{gha4-mali}}

One popular account gives a main mound of 33 hectares, 25 satellite mounds making 69 hectares in all, and up to about 27,000 people around AD 800, with a mud-brick wall 3.6 m thick at the base and no sign of a ruling elite. {{rd-jj}} The population is an estimate, so keep it as a range [CONTESTED].

The city grew especially after 250 CE, small satellites grew with it, and it declined after 1000 CE as Jenne rose about three kilometres away, until it was abandoned by about 1400. {{gha5-vansina}} [PROBABLE]

The McIntoshes argue for heterarchy, meaning power spread across specialist groups, rather than a single state. {{mcintosh-rwe}} {{standen-jj}} Population figures and the exact chronology remain debated. {{lib}}
Jenne-jeno is the standard counter to two old assumptions: that cities need kings, and that African cities needed Arab or Mediterranean trade to appear.
A method for testing any claim

i: Say the claim in one sentence.
Name the kind of evidence behind each part.
Ask what the evidence cannot tell you, using the blind-spot table.
Check dating problems, such as the radiocarbon plateau.
Write a verdict with a tag, and rewrite the sentence to match.

blocks.title: Worked example: 'Jenne-jeno grew because of the gold trade'
steps: Evidence: archaeology dates the town from about 250 BCE and its growth to the first millennium CE.
Blind spot: archaeology shows when the town grew, not why; no written source survives for its early centuries.
Dating check: regular trans-Saharan trade comes later than the town's growth.
Verdict: the causal claim fails on dates. Rewritten sentence: Jenne-jeno grew without regular trans-Saharan trade, and later joined it [PROBABLE]. {{penn-jj}}

blocks.x: Challenge C2: a museum label says the Nok invented ironworking in Africa around 500 BCE and the Yoruba descend directly from them. Write three sentences that correct it, using at least two tags.

blocks.q: An excavated town has specialist quarters for smiths, potters and traders but no palace or royal burial. Which description fits best?
o: A kingdom ruled by one king
Heterarchy: power spread across specialist groups, as argued for Jenne-jeno
A town that cannot be described at all
blocks.w: Heterarchy names power spread across groups rather than held by one ruler. {{mcintosh-rwe}}

blocks.q: A town had a wall in the first millennium CE. A student writes that the wall shows it had a king. What is this?
o: An inference, which should be labelled as such, since a wall does not by itself show kingship
blocks.w: Jenne-jeno had a wall and no sign of a ruling elite. {{rd-jj}}

i: Jenne-jeno shows urban life without a king and before regular Saharan trade [PROBABLE]. {{penn-jj}}
Test every claim: say it, name the evidence, find the blind spot, tag it, rewrite it.
A cautious rewrite is a skill, not a weakness.

lessons.title: Practice: stress tests for your evidence habits

blocks.x: Work each case before you read the verdict. Each one uses a rule from this module.

blocks.title: Stress tests
head: Claim to test
Rule to apply
Verdict and rewrite
rows: Over 500 Bantu languages prove a single conquest
Languages show shared descent, not conquest; small groups moving over centuries [PROBABLE]
A griot says Sundiata won at Kirina in 1235
Keep the story; the date is a [TRADITIONAL DATE] unless a chronicle or archaeology supports it
A Saharan site with grindstones was a farming village
Not shown without plant remains or pollen
The Kano Chronicle proves eleventh-century events
Written-down tradition, late in its written form [THIN EVIDENCE]
Iron spread from Meroë across Africa
An old view, now largely abandoned [CONTESTED]

blocks.x: In each case the habit is the same. Say what the evidence can prove, say what it cannot, and attach a tag. A claim with no tag is an unfinished sentence.
A second habit is to separate what a source says from what you infer, and to label the inference. A source may say a town had a wall; that the wall means it had a king is your inference.

blocks.title: Worked example: one claim through every rule
steps: Claim: 'Ancient Bantu-speaking ironworkers conquered central Africa in 1000 BCE.'
Words: Bantu is a language family, so 'Bantu-speaking' is fine but says nothing of conquest.
Technology: Bantu speakers without iron existed, so iron and language did not travel together.
Dates: 1000 BCE is one estimate for proto-Bantu, with others near 4,800 years ago [CONTESTED].
Rewrite: Bantu languages spread from the Cameroon borderland over many centuries, through small movements and mixing; when the spread began is [CONTESTED]. {{gha3-bantu}} {{grollemund-001}}

blocks.q: A griot gives a date for a battle. What is the safest tag?
blocks.w: Oral tradition gives approximate dates unless another kind of evidence supports them. {{gha1-vansina}}

blocks.q: You find that a short Wolof word sounds like an ancient Egyptian word with a similar meaning. What can you conclude from that alone?
o: There was a migration from Egypt
Nothing yet: you would need regular sound correspondences across many words
blocks.w: Chance resemblances are common among short words. {{dio-method-006}}

i: Say what the evidence proves, what it cannot, and the tag. {{lib}}
Separate finding from inference, and label the inference.
